title: The Cerska Offensive: Crushing the Eastern Pockets
content:
In February 1993, the VRS Drina Corps launched a major offensive against the Bosniak-held pockets of Cerska and Konjevic Polje in eastern Bosnia. The operation represented a systematic effort to eliminate the chain of besieged enclaves along the Drina valley, and its execution demonstrated both the overwhelming military advantage the VRS held in the region and the near-total absence of international protection for the civilian populations trapped within.

The eastern Bosnian enclaves had existed in a state of semi-siege since the summer of 1992. Bosniak populations driven from surrounding municipalities by ethnic cleansing campaigns had concentrated in a series of small pockets — Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje — that maintained tenuous connections through difficult mountain terrain. These pockets lacked heavy weapons, consistent supply lines, and any realistic prospect of relief from the main body of the ARBiH, separated by dozens of kilometres of VRS-controlled territory.

The Drina Corps offensive, supported by armour and artillery that included assets from the Yugoslav Army across the Serbian border, advanced rapidly against positions that could not withstand sustained conventional assault. Cerska fell in early March. Konjevic Polje followed shortly after. The offensive severed the land connection between the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, reducing Srebrenica's accessible territory to roughly 150 square kilometres. Tens of thousands of displaced people were driven into the already overcrowded Srebrenica pocket, where humanitarian conditions were catastrophic.

The ICTY addressed the Drina valley campaign in multiple proceedings. The Krstic Trial Judgment (IT-98-33-T), while centred on the 1995 genocide, established the broader operational pattern of the Drina Corps in eastern Bosnia, including the progressive reduction of Bosniak-held territory through military offensives combined with the restriction of humanitarian access. The Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T) examined command responsibility for operations across eastern Bosnia as part of a wider pattern of persecution and forcible transfer directed against the Bosniak population of the Drina valley.

The fall of Cerska triggered an international response that, while inadequate, set important precedents. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 819 on 16 April 1993, declaring Srebrenica a Safe Area — the first application of the concept that would subsequently be extended to Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zepa, Gorazde, and Bihac under Resolution 836. The gap between the protective language of these resolutions and the resources committed to enforce them would prove to be one of the defining failures of the international response.

Militarily, the Cerska offensive demonstrated a pattern the VRS would repeat throughout the conflict: the use of overwhelming conventional superiority against isolated, lightly armed pockets, combined with the deliberate restriction of humanitarian access to create conditions of deprivation. The offensive also illustrated the strategic logic driving the Bosnian Serb campaign in the Drina valley — the elimination of Bosniak population centres along the border with Serbia, consistent with the third of the Six Strategic Goals adopted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly in May 1992.

The survivors of Cerska and Konjevic Polje joined the swelling population of Srebrenica, where they would endure two more years of siege before the enclave's catastrophic fall in July 1995. The February-March offensive of 1993 was not the end of the eastern enclaves, but it established the military and humanitarian conditions that made their eventual destruction possible.
